1:
The image in the first verse is understood as irrigation by four of them, and they differ only in what is being watered. Adam Clarke describes the practice, several canals dug from one stream so that by opening a particular sluice the husbandman directs the water where he pleases, and applies it to royal favour: as the land is enriched by the streams, so is the king’s favourite by the royal bounty, and God can induce him to bestow it on whom he will. Charles Ellicott reads it the same way, of a heart turned now toward one suppliant and now toward another. John Wesley gives the practice in a line. Matthew Henry uses the figure for a different purpose, to protect the will: the husbandman turning water through his grounds does not alter the nature of the water nor put any force upon it, any more than providence does upon the native freedom of man’s will, and yet the course is directed to serve the purpose intended. John Gill alone abandons the irrigation and takes the water for instability, the heart of a king being unstable, fluid and fluctuating, which God can nevertheless settle and keep within bounds.

On the preference of justice to sacrifice, Keil and Delitzsch place the saying in a tradition, observing how greatly this depreciation of the ceremonial works beside the duties of moral obedience belongs to the spirit of the wisdom writings, that prophecy gives the same testimony, and that what is required here is not legal rigour but the equitable and good, conduct proceeding at bottom from the principle of love. Henry draws a larger inference from the same comparison: sacrifices were of divine institution and acceptable when offered in faith, yet even then moral duties were preferred before them, which intimates that their excellence was not innate nor the obligation to them perpetual. He also names the self-deception the proverb answers, of men who suppose that offering sacrifice will excuse them from doing justice.

The fourth verse contains the chapter’s hardest word, and four senses are proposed. Ellicott renders it the work of the wicked, all they do, since it is done to please themselves and in reliance on their own strength, though he allows the word may also signify a lamp. Clarke takes the lamp and reads it as the prosperity and posterity of the wicked, evil in the seed and in the root and in the branch and in the fruit. Wesley makes it their civil and natural actions, lawful in themselves but made sinful by being managed without regard to God’s glory. Henry uses both readings in one note, having the wicked always ploughing and plotting and then saying that the light of the wicked is sin. Keil and Delitzsch canvass every option at length and reach no conclusion, rejecting brilliant prosperity and a flaming proud spirit as contrary to the usual force of the metaphor, and rejecting the meaning yoke because it is not Hebrew but belongs to the neighbouring tongues. On the next verse they and Ellicott independently gather the same cluster of sayings from three languages about haste and speed, Keil and Delitzsch adding a modern poet’s lines about revolving like the stars without haste but without rest. Henry compresses it to a maxim, that forecast is as good as work. On the last verse of the section, Clarke reports that several manuscripts, some ancient editions and four versions read the snares of death rather than those who seek death, so that the sense becomes pursuing vanity into the snares of death; Keil and Delitzsch report the same divided evidence and say plainly that the text is unsettled.
7:
The verb of the seventh verse has three homonyms behind it, and the versions take all three. Keil and Delitzsch set the evidence out: one old Latin translator and one Greek render it teareth or draggeth away, which they judge right; the older Greek version derived it instead from a root meaning to dwell or to live as a guest; and two others took it from a root meaning to dread, so that the violence terrifies the violent. Adam Clarke follows the third and has the wicked terrified and ruined by the means they used to aggrandise themselves. John Gill produces a fourth on a Jewish commentator’s authority, that the word means to saw or dissect, so that conscience draws a saw to and fro over such men. Charles Ellicott simply renders the noun their violence. Matthew Henry is interested in the moral rather than the root, and states it sharply: getting money by lying is no better than downright robbery, since cheating is stealing, and a man might as well pick another’s pocket as impose on him by a lie in making a bargain; those who refuse to do justice will end by choosing to do wrong.

On the next verse two of them abandon the received rendering. Keil and Delitzsch, noting that the first word occurs only here, connect the second through a neighbouring language with being charged with a crime, and render the line, winding is the way of a man laden with guilt; Ellicott offers the same as an alternative. Henry keeps strange and works it three ways, that such a man’s way is contrary to all rules of honour and honesty, that it is strange because you know neither where to find him nor when you have him, and that it is strange because alienated from all good. John Wesley makes it estranged from God. The verse about the housetop is unsettled at the other end. Keil and Delitzsch hold the phrase to mean a house in common, the joining of the wife and the house by a conjunction being a figure in which two ideas are set side by side where our own language would subordinate one to the other. Clarke gives the same sense as a house of fellowship, what we should call a lodging-house occupied by several families, and adds that some think a house of festivity is meant, his own old English manuscript Bible having the house and feast. Henry keeps the wide house and gets his point from the word itself, since it means a house of society in which a man may entertain his friends, and the affliction described makes both him and his house unsociable. Ellicott lists what those flat roofs were used for, exercise, sleeping, devotion and domestic purposes.

Keil and Delitzsch find the interchange of tenses in the following verse deliberate, the perfect stating what is actually the case, that the desire of such a man is settled upon evil as his general nature and tendency, and the future stating what proceeds from it, that whoever stands near him is not spared. On the punishment of the scorner, they observe that the mocker himself is incorrigible and gains nothing by it, yet the punishment is not lost, since as a warning example it teaches the simple who might otherwise be drawn into the same frivolity. Henry draws a rule from that, that it is no injustice to take to ourselves a good lesson designed for another. Clarke agrees that one such public example is a blessing to thousands, and then sets a limit that no one else here approaches: only blasphemy against God and the Bible should be so punished, and private opinion the state should not meddle with.
13:
The first verse of this section produces an instructive contrast of method. Keil and Delitzsch pause over a single preposition in it and confess that no preposition of their own language nor of ours expresses so full a meaning; Adam Clarke refers the reader to the priest and the Levite who passed by the wounded man and then closes the matter in a sentence, that the words are quite plain and there is no difficulty here. Matthew Henry supplies the picture instead, of a man who resolves to take no notice of the cry, turns the poor from his door, and if he cannot avoid hearing will at least not heed; and states the doom, that he shall himself be reduced to straits which make him cry, and then not be heard.

The verb of the following verse is genuinely difficult. Keil and Delitzsch report that one scholar, with three ancient versions, renders it extinguishes anger, and explain how that sense could arise, since the word there means to cover by turning something over, as one turns a vessel upside down, which done to a candle amounts to putting it out; but the same word also means to bend and so to force down, between which two senses a Jewish commentator hesitated. John Gill takes the extinguishing on the authority of two versions and finds it very fitting, since anger is a fire in the breast, though he notes that others render it bringing the anger down. On the transaction itself Henry describes its manners exactly: it must be a gift in secret and a reward in the bosom, because the taker would not be thought to covet it, nor known to receive it, nor be willingly beholden to a man he has been offended with, but if it is done privately all is well. He adds that covetousness is commonly a master-sin with command of the other lusts. Gill notes that some understand the verse of a bribe given to a judge, and John Wesley observes that the secrecy is what makes such a gift acceptable; none of them will say whether the proverb approves what it describes.

The second half of the fifteenth verse is read two ways, and both are pointed. Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take it that doing right is itself a terror to the workers of iniquity, who are afraid they will be ruined if they do not cheat their neighbours when they have opportunity, injustice having become to them a second nature. Henry offers both this and the plainer sense, that it terrifies them to see the laws executed against vice. On the congregation the wanderer joins, three destinations are named. Henry makes it the sinners of the old world swept away by the flood, and observes that such a man shall rest but not in peace. Clarke agrees and enlarges: the word means the lost, and the passage intimates that they are in a state of conscious existence, though the congregation may also include the fallen angels; he quotes his old English manuscript Bible on the same verse. Ellicott takes it forward instead, that such a man shall have no part in the resurrection, and calls the verse a prophecy of retribution after death. On the love of pleasure Clarke is severest, naming the sports pursued when a man should be attending to the culture of his fields and adding that he shall be so deservedly poor as to have none to pity him; Henry allows the lawful use of these things soberly and temperately and locates the fault in setting the heart on them. Ellicott turns to prices, and reckons what a pound of the ointment named in the Gospels would have cost in his own money, about a year’s wages of a day labourer.
19:
The section opens with a saying that repeats one already given, and Keil and Delitzsch notice both the repetition and a remark made about it. Treating the verse as the point where the collector begins a new addition, they report a scholar’s witticism that the corner of the roof having already been used, the author must now look further out for a lonely seat — and dismiss it in a sentence as piquant but devoid of thought, since it assumes without asking whether both proverbs have the same author and, if so, whether they were coined at the same time. John Gill extracts a joke of his own from the noun, observing that the word for wilderness may signify the place where no speech is, so that a man without a voice near him is preferred to a voice that scolds. Matthew Henry states the principle: those cannot dwell in peace and happiness who cannot dwell in peace and love, and even those who are one flesh, if they are not also one spirit, have no joy of their union.

On the treasure and oil of the next verse Keil and Delitzsch dispute the pointing, denying that the words can be rendered a treasure of what is precious and oil, since the vowels forbid it. John Wesley explains why oil is singled out, being a considerable part of the wealth of those countries; Henry adds a domestic preference of his own, that it is better to have an old-fashioned house well furnished than a fine modern one with sorry housekeeping. The verse that follows sets a puzzle, since righteousness is both what is pursued and what is found. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two things pursued, the first being conduct proceeding from the principle of self-denying love which is the essence of the law, and the second conduct proceeding from sympathy, which puts itself in another’s place, perceives what will benefit him, and sets about doing it. Charles Ellicott resolves the repetition by reading the three rewards twice over, first as length of days, power to live more uprightly, and present honour from God and man, and then in a higher sense as eternal life, the forgiveness of sins, and honour at the last day. Henry resolves it more simply, that God gives such men grace to do good and the pleasure of doing it.

The wise man who takes a city is read as a soldier by some and as something else by Henry. Adam Clarke keeps to siegecraft and remarks what skill does in the fortification and reduction of strong places; Keil and Delitzsch cite the parallel of the poor wise man who delivered a besieged town; Gill applies it to Christ entering a heart held by the strong man armed. Henry converts the whole figure, holding that a wise man will gain upon the affections of people and conquer them by strength of reason, which is a nobler conquest than any got by strength of arms. On guarding the mouth Henry offers a two-way rule, that keeping the heart will keep the tongue from sin and keeping the tongue will keep the heart from trouble. The last verse of the section draws from Keil and Delitzsch the most unexpected note in the chapter: the word rendered scorner is an old one meaning properly the distorter, and they say that as in the west since the previous century the names of free-thinkers have become current for those who subject the faith of the church to destructive criticism, so then this name was given to men who mockingly, as though of full age, set themselves above revealed religion and prophecy. Henry describes the same men as making anger their trade, having nothing so much to do as to barter passions and exchange bitter words.
25:
Keil and Delitzsch correct a scholar on the opening verse with unusual precision. He had said that the sluggard’s desire goes out first after meat and drink, and that in that direction, as hunger, it kills him indeed; to which they answer that in that case it is not the desire which kills him but the impossibility of satisfying it, and that what the proverb means is that the inordinate longing after rest and pleasure brings him at last to ruin. They add that almost all interpreters join this verse and the next into a single four-line saying. Matthew Henry puts the same double bind in an image: besides that their slothfulness starves them, their desires at the same time stab them, for though the hands refuse to labour the heart does not cease to covet riches and pleasures and honours, which cannot be had without labour, and they cry give, give, expecting everybody to do for them.

The clause about bringing a sacrifice with a wicked mind draws two of them to the same sharp reading. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the preposition is not one of manner, since the godless man’s general way of life is not in question, but one of price: the sacrifice is brought as payment for the crime intended. Charles Ellicott reaches the same place independently, that the offerer is plotting future wickedness or thinking to make God overlook his sin by the gift, and so become as it were his confederate. Adam Clarke adds the cases where the offering is of goods ill-gotten or made by constraint of custom, and John Wesley that it is offered to cover or countenance some wicked design. Henry puts the whole matter in a sentence, that many can freely give God their beasts, their lips and their knees who would not give him their hearts.

The line about the man who hears is genuinely obscure, and Keil and Delitzsch make short work of a conjecture about it. The Greek version read a man who guards himself, one scholar supposed a different word behind that, and another emended further to get the man who rejoices to deliver — at which they ask where in all the world the verb in question means to deliver, and give their own sense, that the man meant hears before he speaks. Ellicott resolves the adverb differently and more attractively, glossing that he who hears carefully and repeats accurately speaks constantly in the sense that his testimony will live after him. Wesley takes constantly to mean that he always affirms the same thing. On the next verse Clarke reports that upwards of fifty manuscripts of two collators, with several ancient editions and some versions, read that the upright man understands his way rather than directs it, and that because he understands it he is able to direct himself in it; Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same variant and prefer the marginal reading. Henry gets the moral from the contrast: the wicked man asks what would I do and what have I a mind to, while the upright asks what should I do, what does God require of me, and so does not force his way but directs it. On the last verse Clarke notices an irony in the ascription of the book, since horses were not used by that people before the reign of the king named in its title, a divine command having forbidden them, and that king transgressed it — yet here he allows that a horse is a vain thing for safety. John Gill takes the horse as standing for all other military preparation, and Keil and Delitzsch that it remains with God to give the victory or not.
